title: Uncomfortable Truth: Disrupting the Childcare Status Quo is Satisfying, but Not Easy
author: Asayya Imaya
excerpt: Uthabiti Africa was born from an uncomfortable belief: Africa’s childcare crisis is too large, too complex and too important to be left to a few organisations to solve. It was an ambitious proposition when we began. It…
paragraphs: Uthabiti Africa was born from an uncomfortable belief: Africa’s childcare crisis is too large, too complex and too important to be left to a few organisations to solve. It was an ambitious proposition when we began. It remained one as the work continued. That is why collective action was at the centre of our vision and mission from the word go. One word that kept coming up was – ‘disruption’.

How could we positively disrupt the ecosystem and lead to the growth of the childcare ecosystem? Over the years, we have learned that disrupting a system is not easy. Systems develop habits. Institutions develop ways of working. People become accustomed to who leads, who funds, who decides and whose voice is heard. Vested interests can be embedded in every conversation, and it is always not easy to decipher.

Many cards can be under the table. When this happens, the achievement of accelerated quality, affordable childcare is delayed. That is why disruption was central to Uthabiti’s early identity. We challenged the idea that childcare was simply a private or social issue and began positioning it as essential economic and social infrastructure. We brought together actors who had rarely been in the same conversation, created new platforms for collaboration, tested new models, and opened the ecosystem to voices and actors who had previously been overlooked.

In the process, we learnt that changing established patterns takes patience and persistence. It requires the courage to ask uncomfortable questions, the humility to test, learn and sometimes start again, and the conviction to keep going when change is not immediately visible. But it is also deeply satisfying. Because change rarely happens all at once. It happens when another voice enters the conversation.

When an organisation that once saw childcare as someone else’s responsibility begins to see itself as part of the solution. When a caregiver gains recognition and a stronger voice. When a government actor takes greater ownership. When a provider sees a pathway to grow. When an idea that once seemed impossible begins to move towards scale. Each of these moments shifts the ecosystem. And that is the disruption Uthabiti set out to pursue.

Not disruption for its own sake, but disruption that changes what is possible — changing the way childcare is understood, who gets to shape it, and how the ecosystem comes together to make change happen. But disruption of a childcare status quo that is simply not sufficient for the scale of Africa’s needs. The uncomfortable truth For decades, much of the childcare agenda has been shaped by a relatively small number of institutions, programmes and funders.

They are usually very well-connected and have learnt just how to tell their story the right way, with the right words. At times, because there was so little happening, we learnt to celebrate almost everything that was happening. Because it was important to elevate those who were making an effort. The important thing is that many organisations were making important contributions, at times with limited resources or only the commitment to do the right thing for children and caregivers.

As a result, their collective effort brought childcare onto policy agendas, generated evidence, supported caregivers, developed programmes and demonstrated what is possible. But the awareness of the challenge, the success of disruption has made it clear that in Kenya, demand for action has, over the last 7 years of Uthabiti’s work – has grown beyond what any small group of organisations can address. Uthabiti started from the premise that the childcare crisis in Africa is an emergency.

I still think this is the case. Because across the continent, childcare is a crisis. Urgent action is required, now. The uncomfortable truth is that 7 years later, it is not yet an emergency for many countries in Africa. In 2022, I drove from Nairobi to Malawi and back, literally exploring how to scale collective action on childcare by road! Having spent many years outside Africa, I was amazed at HOW urbanization was changing the face of Kenya, Tanzania, Malawi .

From Nairobi, through Arusha, Mbeya, Lilongwe and Blantyre, I realized Africa was urbanizing fast. An in every future city I saw, I wondered where childcare sat in that rapid development. I wondered whether, like in Kenya, there were only a few organisations who controlled the narrative and many others who struggled to get things done, The reality is Africa's changing demographics, rapid urbanisation, women's growing participation in the economy, changing family structures and persistent inequalities are creating new and urgent demands for childcare.

At the same time, millions of children need safe and nurturing care, while the people providing that care often remain poorly paid, under-recognised and outside formal systems. The uncomfortable truth that has persistently emerged over the last 7 years is that the crisis is simply too big for business as usual. And that continuously raises a difficult question: What if the problem is not only that we need more childcare—but that we need a fundamentally different childcare ecosystem?

Uthabiti was created to disrupt and help open that ecosystem. We wanted to challenge the idea that childcare solutions must come from a limited number of organisations and that everyone else is simply a beneficiary, implementer or recipient. What if childcare workers could be solution-makers? What if providers could be micro-entrepreneurs? What if parents could shape services? What if caregivers were trained and organized?

What if businesses saw childcare as an economic opportunity? What if governments could accelerate policy and regulatory reforms? What if governments were supported to lead systems rather than simply implement projects? And what if these actors could connect, learn from one another and act collectively? These questions sit at the heart of Uthabiti's work. Our role has continued to be focused on helping create the platforms, evidence, relationships, capabilities and practical models that allow more people and institutions to participate in shaping the future of childcare.

From childcare programme to childcare ecosystem This is also why Uthabiti approaches childcare through a market systems lens. We believe childcare is not simply a social service. It is part of the infrastructure that allows economies and societies to function. Childcare enables parents to work. It is a public services, a public good that needs to be elevated. It enables women to participate more fully in economic life.

It creates jobs. It creates opportunities for enterprise. It creates demand for training, infrastructure, services and innovation. And it can generate better livelihoods for the people whose work makes childcare possible. But these opportunities will not emerge automatically. They require functioning systems: appropriate policies, investment, capable providers, a professional workforce, information, standards, financing, infrastructure and strong relationships between the actors who shape the market.

That is why our ambition is not simply to establish more childcare projects. It is to help build a childcare ecosystem capable of producing, sustaining and scaling many solutions. Disruption is not about replacing people. One lesson has become particularly clear. Disruption does not mean replacing one set of actors with another. It means changing the conditions under which everyone operates.

We do not need fewer organisations working on childcare. We need more capable organisations. More providers. More entrepreneurs. More researchers. More investors. More government leadership. More caregiver voices. More community participation. We need an ecosystem where different actors can bring different capabilities to a common challenge. That is why collective-action platforms matter.

It is why we created Collaborative Action for Childcare (CAC). It is why we invest in convening. It is why we generate evidence and engage governments. It is why we work on workforce development through initiatives such as MamaPlus. And it is why we are interested in strengthening the economic agency and organisation of childcare workers. Each is a different piece of a much bigger system.

Satisfying, but not easy There have been moments when this approach would have been easier if we had simply chosen a narrower lane. It is easier to run a programme than to try to change the conditions around it. It is easier to deliver training than to ask whether the workforce system itself needs to change. It is easier to implement a project than to bring government, workers, providers, families, businesses, researchers and funders into a shared conversation.

It is easier to celebrate a successful pilot than to ask what it would take for that solution to survive, adapt and scale beyond the pilot. Systems change asks harder questions. It takes longer. It requires collaboration across organisational boundaries. It requires being willing to share ownership. And it requires accepting that sometimes the most important outcome is not that Uthabiti gets credit, but that the system gets stronger.

That is not always easy. But it is satisfying. Because the moments that matter are not only the ones where Uthabiti achieves something itself. They are the moments when the ecosystem begins to move. When a caregiver sees a pathway to professional growth. When a provider sees an opportunity to strengthen and expand. When government sees childcare differently. When an entrepreneur sees a market where previously there was only a social problem.

When organisations that previously worked separately discover what they can accomplish together. When an idea moves from a conversation to a practical solution. When a solution begins to move towards scale.That is the change we want to see. The work ahead We are still far from where we need to be in Africa. The continent does not yet have childcare systems that match the scale of its economic and social ambitions.

But perhaps the most important shift is already underway: more people are beginning to recognise that childcare is not somebody else’s problem. It belongs to all of us. Governments must lead. Markets have a role. Communities have a role. Families have a role. Workers have a role. Researchers, businesses, investors and civil society all have a role. And organisations like Uthabiti have a role in helping connect these capabilities, create the platforms for collaboration and support the conditions in which more actors can contribute.

The childcare crisis is too big for a few organisations. But that does not mean it is too big to change. It means we need to change the way we come together to change it. That has been at the heart of Uthabiti’s journey: not to build another organisation at the centre of childcare, but to help build a stronger ecosystem around it. Satisfying, but not easy. And very much still underway.

The conversation then moved from disruption to action through the Second Africa Childcare Forum in Mombasa. The Second Africa Childcare Forum, ACFMombasa2026, brought together people and institutions with a role in shaping what came next. Because if the childcare status quo is going to change, the question is no longer simply what needs to change? It is: what were we prepared to build together?

title: What If Childcare Was Africa’s Next Great Economic Opportunity?
author: Asayya Imaya
excerpt: Following the 2nd Africa Childcare Forum in Mombasa, the question was no longer simply whether childcare was an economic opportunity. The Forum helped bring renewed attention to what it would take to realise that…
paragraphs: Following the 2nd Africa Childcare Forum in Mombasa, the question was no longer simply whether childcare was an economic opportunity. The Forum helped bring renewed attention to what it would take to realise that opportunity. The question was whether we could build the systems needed to realise that opportunity—and whether we could do so together. What If Childcare Is Africa’s Next Great Economic Opportunity?

For much of the development conversation, childcare has been framed as a social need with an economic cost. Families struggle to afford it. Governments face difficult choices about public spending, including how to balance investment in human capital and physical infrastructure. Employers are asked to consider how they can support workers with young children. Development organisations fund programmes to expand access, improve quality and strengthen the childcare workforce.

These conversations are necessary, and Uthabiti Africa has been at the forefront of advancing them. Yet, taken together, they reveal a persistent way of thinking about childcare: as something society needs to pay for. There is another way to look at it. Childcare is not simply an expense incurred by families or a service requiring public investment. It is part of the infrastructure that allows economies to function.

It enables parents to work, influences whether women can enter and progress in the labour market, creates employment for childcare workers and sustains a network of providers and businesses. It also generates demand for training, infrastructure, food, equipment, finance and other services. With the right market and institutional conditions, childcare can become a source of enterprise, innovation and investment.

The question is no longer whether childcare has economic value. It is whether Africa is organising its childcare economy in ways that allow that value to be realised. Across much of the continent, childcare remains fragmented. Families make their own arrangements, communities fill gaps, and women undertake enormous amounts of unpaid care. Private and community providers deliver much of the available childcare, often with varying degrees of formality.

Caregivers frequently work without recognised qualifications or clear career pathways. Governments are developing policies and standards, but implementation and financing remain uneven. Deliberate, coordinated action to strengthen childcare systems is still limited. This needs to change. An economy already exists around childcare. What is missing is a sufficiently strong market system to make it more productive, sustainable and inclusive.

That is where the opportunity lies. The economy cannot work without care Every economy depends on people being able to participate in it. And people cannot participate without someone caring for those who depend on them. Yet economic policy has historically treated paid work as productive and much of the care that makes it possible as a private household responsibility. This thinking is reflected in statements heard across the continent: children should not be in childcare centres; they should be at home with their mothers.

Such views overlook the realities of changing African societies. More mothers and fathers are working, families are migrating to cities, and traditional extended-family support systems are changing as nuclear households become more common. The need for reliable childcare is growing, even as the arrangements families have historically depended on become less available. A parent can leave home to work because a neighbour provides childcare for a small fee.

A nurse can report for a shift because arrangements have been made for her children. A trader can spend the day running her business because somebody is providing care. An employee can accept a job with demanding hours because childcare has been secured through a domestic worker. The setting may be a home, a centre, a community, a workplace or an informal arrangement. Whatever its form, childcare performs an essential economic function.

This is particularly important for women's economic participation. Across Africa, women are active in formal employment, professional occupations, farming, trading, household enterprises and other forms of informal work. Yet the unequal distribution of unpaid care continues to shape the choices available to them. When affordable and reliable childcare is unavailable, a mother may turn down employment, reduce her working hours, choose work closer to home, accept lower earnings in exchange for flexibility or rely on unpaid support from another woman in the family.

These decisions may not appear in labour-market statistics as childcare problems, but childcare can be a significant factor behind them. Economic empowerment cannot be separated from the conditions under which people organise their time. We have become comfortable talking about access to finance, entrepreneurship, skills and employment as drivers of women's economic participation.

Yet these interventions can have limited impact when the care infrastructure surrounding women's economic lives remains weak. A woman can receive business training and a loan and still struggle to grow her enterprise if she is simultaneously responsible for caring for young children throughout the day. This does not make childcare a women's issue alone. It makes it an economic systems issue.

A society that wants more people to participate productively in the economy must consider the infrastructure that makes that participation possible. Childcare belongs in that conversation. Childcare is more than an enabler of work There is another dimension to the economic argument that deserves equal attention: childcare is not only infrastructure supporting other economic activity.

It is an economic activity in its own right. Across African cities, towns and communities, people already earn livelihoods providing care. Childcare centres, home-based providers, nannies, community-based services and early childhood practitioners form part of a diverse landscape of provision. Around them are training institutions, suppliers, landlords, food businesses, manufacturers, transport operators and increasingly, technology and financial-service providers.

This is a market, even where it does not resemble one in the conventional sense. The challenge is that much of this activity operates informally and in isolation. A provider may have strong demand from families but little access to working capital. A caregiver may have years of experience but no recognised qualification. A training institution may offer courses without clear connections to employment opportunities.

Families may pay for services without reliable information to assess quality. Financial institutions may regard providers as too small or informal to serve. Regulators may establish standards that small providers struggle to meet without appropriate support. The result is a paradox: significant demand and substantial economic activity can coexist with a poorly functioning market. This is where the distinction between a market and a functioning market system becomes important.

The objective should not simply be to create more childcare businesses, nor should we assume that commercial growth will automatically deliver better childcare. We need to understand what prevents the existing childcare economy from functioning more effectively. As we built our Caregiver Network, we began asking important questions. What makes it difficult for providers to become viable and improve quality?

Why are childcare skills so poorly rewarded? What prevents finance from reaching providers? How can families obtain better information? What forms of regulation protect children without making formal provision inaccessible to small operators? Where should government intervene, and where can enterprise and investment play a greater role? How can childcare workers organise and engage collectively to help shape effective regulation?

These questions go beyond counting childcare centres. Our Caregiver Network now has 7,300 members and continues to grow. But a network alone is not enough. Its value lies in helping us understand the underlying structures, relationships and constraints that shape the sector. The workforce reflects the weaknesses of the system Our Network members have consistently highlighted the challenges facing childcare workers.

Many receive low wages, have limited employment security and face few opportunities for advancement. Training can be disconnected from recognised occupational pathways, while years of practical experience do not always translate into formal recognition. Providers, meanwhile, may struggle to pay a better-qualified workforce because families cannot afford higher fees. This creates a vicious cycle.

Care work has traditionally been associated with women's unpaid domestic responsibilities. That history continues to influence how paid care work is valued. Childcare is often regarded as something women are naturally capable of doing rather than as a skilled occupation requiring knowledge, judgement, professional standards and continuing development. When the work is poorly valued, investment in skills is limited.

When skills are not consistently recognised, workers have limited bargaining power. Financially constrained providers struggle to improve wages, making it harder to attract and retain people who see childcare as a profession rather than temporary employment. The answer cannot simply be to train more people while leaving everything else unchanged. Professionalising childcare requires a functioning workforce system: recognised qualifications, credible occupational pathways, employer demand, appropriate remuneration, continuing professional development, better working conditions and opportunities for progression.

This is one reason workforce development is central to Uthabiti Africa's work. Through MamaPlus and the MamaPlus Training Centre, our focus extends beyond training individual caregivers to addressing the wider conditions that can make childcare work more professional, better recognised and economically viable. The same principle applies across the sector. Families, providers, workers, government and investors are interconnected, and weaknesses in one part of the system constrain the performance of the whole.

The opportunity is therefore not simply to create more businesses or attract more investment. It is to build a functioning childcare market system in which families can access appropriate services, providers can operate sustainably, workers can build careers, enterprises can innovate, governments can regulate and invest effectively, and capital can reach viable opportunities without compromising the purpose of childcare. From economic opportunity to collective action Realising this opportunity requires a different conversation.

We need to move beyond asking how much childcare costs and begin asking what kind of childcare economy Africa wants to build. What would make childcare a viable sector for decent work and enterprise? How can public investment encourage rather than displace private and community provision? How can finance reach the thousands of small providers already serving families? How can regulation protect children while enabling providers to improve and formalise?

How can workforce development create genuine occupational pathways rather than certificates with little economic value? And how can governments, businesses, investors, workers and communities contribute to a stronger system? No single organisation can answer these questions. They require different perspectives, expertise and forms of collaboration, grounded in a shared understanding of the challenges and the practical changes needed to address them.

That is the role of collective action in childcare: not simply bringing stakeholders into the same room, but creating the conditions for them to understand their interdependence and act on it. This was among the conversations advanced through the 2nd Africa Childcare Forum, ACFMombasa2026. If childcare is essential infrastructure for Africa's economies, it cannot remain at the margins of economic policy, labour-market thinking, enterprise development and investment.

And if childcare is itself an economic sector, we must become more deliberate about building the market systems that enable it to grow, create decent work, improve quality and remain responsive to the needs of children and families. The Forum provided an opportunity to bring these questions into one conversation, not because everyone arrived with the same answers, but because the answers needed to connect. Governments bring policy authority and public investment.

Providers bring practical knowledge of delivering care. Caregivers understand the realities of the workforce. Families understand the constraints of affordability and access. Businesses and investors can contribute capital, innovation and new models. Researchers can strengthen the evidence base, while development partners can help test and finance approaches that public and private actors can eventually sustain.

None of these contributions is sufficient on its own. The opportunity lies in how they connect. A market-systems perspective asks whether the relationships, incentives, institutions, policies, financing and capabilities surrounding childcare are strong enough for the sector to function and evolve. Africa does not need childcare markets at any cost. It needs markets that work for children, families, workers and the wider economy.

The opportunity is much bigger than creating another category of businesses. It is about building the infrastructure, institutions and markets that allow childcare to become a stronger part of Africa's social and economic fabric. That is a conversation worth having across the continent. What Needed to Happen Next? Recognising childcare as an economic opportunity is an important starting point.

Realising that opportunity requires something more: a deliberate effort to build the systems that enable the childcare economy to function, grow and deliver value for children, families, workers and businesses. This means moving beyond isolated interventions towards a more connected approach. Governments must be able to translate policy into effective regulation, financing and implementation.

Providers need pathways to improve quality, strengthen their businesses and access appropriate finance. Caregivers need recognised skills, decent working conditions and opportunities for professional growth. Families need affordable, reliable services, while investors and businesses need to understand both the potential of the childcare economy and the conditions required for it to thrive.

These are not separate challenges. They are interconnected parts of the same system. Progress in one area will remain constrained if the others are neglected. This is where collective action becomes essential. The 2nd Africa Childcare Forum (ACF), Mombasa 2026, brought these different perspectives together around a shared question: What will it take to build childcare systems and markets that work for Africa?

Under the theme “Uniting for Care: Africa’s Call to the World,” the Forum provided an opportunity for governments, childcare providers, workers, businesses, investors, researchers and development partners to move beyond recognising the importance of care and examine what needs to change in practice. The task is not simply to encourage more childcare businesses or attract investment into the sector. It is to identify the policy, institutional, financial and workforce conditions that will enable childcare to become a viable, inclusive and sustainable part of Africa’s economic infrastructure—without losing sight of the quality of care that children deserve.

No single organisation could build this system alone. Nor could one Forum resolve every constraint. But collective action helped establish a shared understanding of the challenges, connect actors who have previously worked in isolation, identify opportunities for collaboration and create momentum for practical, locally owned solutions. That is the ambition behind ACF: to strengthen the connections between policy and practice, evidence and investment, and the people who provide care and the institutions that shape its future.

Africa’s childcare opportunity is already here. The question is whether we can organise ourselves to realise it. In Mombasa, the conversation moved beyond why childcare mattered towards what needed to be built together to make it work.

title: (Re)designing the Childcare Workforce
author: Asayya Imaya
excerpt: When Uthabiti started in 2019, it became very clear that the childcare workforce was immensely under-developed, not just in Kenya but across the continent. Then the big reality hit: there was some training but it was…
paragraphs: When Uthabiti started in 2019, it became very clear that the childcare workforce was immensely under-developed, not just in Kenya but across the continent. Then the big reality hit: there was some training but it was being done using multiple different curricular. Sourced from different countries. England. Canada. USA. Australia. We quickly realized, alongside other actors within the ecosystem that Africa could not possibly professionalise childcare by simply training more caregivers into the same system that was broken from the very foundations.

The question was: How could we have reached here in the first place while investing more heavily in basic and tertiary education? When we spoke about childcare, the conversation often quickly turned to training. Caregivers need better skills. Training programmes need to improve. Qualifications need to be developed. Standards need to be established. All of this mattered. But it was not not enough.

Not without professionalizing the workforce. A workforce becomes a profession not simply because people have been trained, but because there is a system around their work that recognises what they do, establishes expectations for practice, creates pathways for progression and gives workers a meaningful stake in the development of their profession. This is where the childcare workforce challenge becomes more complex.

Across Africa, thousands of people care for young children every day, yet childcare work is often poorly defined as an occupation. Many workers enter the field without formal preparation, acquire skills through experience, and remain in roles with little recognition of that experience. Qualifications are not always connected to clear occupational pathways, and opportunities for progression are limited.

The result is a workforce that exists at scale without a corresponding professional system around it. If Africa is serious about improving the quality and consistency of childcare, that has to change. The question is therefore not simply: How do we train more caregivers? It is: What kind of workforce system would enable childcare workers to enter, develop, advance and remain in the profession?

From care work to recognised work The status of childcare work is deeply connected to how societies have historically understood care. Much of the care provided to young children has been unpaid and undertaken within families, predominantly by women. When care becomes paid work, some of the assumptions attached to unpaid domestic care can follow it into the labour market. The work may require patience, judgement, observation, communication, responsibility and an understanding of children's development.

Yet it can still be treated as work that women simply know how to do. This creates a fundamental contradiction. We expect childcare workers to take responsibility for the safety, wellbeing and development of young children, while often giving them limited professional recognition or opportunity to develop their expertise. Professionalisation begins by challenging that contradiction.

It means recognising childcare as skilled work. It means defining competencies, establishing standards of practice and creating credible pathways through which experience and learning can be recognised. It means creating a clearer distinction between someone who happens to provide care and someone who has developed the knowledge and capabilities to practise childcare professionally.

This distinction matters for workers, but it also matters for children. A profession creates shared expectations about what good practice looks like. It provides a basis for supervision and accountability. It creates mechanisms for continuing development. And it gives workers a professional identity through which they can understand their responsibilities and their own development. The objective is not to make childcare unnecessarily bureaucratic.

It is to create enough structure around the occupation for quality and professional growth to become possible. Training is the beginning, not the destination There is an important difference between training people for childcare work and building a childcare profession. Training focuses on what an individual knows or can do. Workforce development asks what happens to that person before, during and after training.

A caregiver may complete a course. But is the qualification recognised? Does it correspond to an occupational level? Can previous experience be assessed and recognised? What happens when the caregiver wants to advance? Is there a pathway into supervision, management, mentoring or training? Can the worker access continuing professional development? Are there institutions that represent the profession and contribute to setting its standards?

These questions determine whether training becomes part of a functioning workforce system or remains an isolated intervention. This is why curriculum development and certification are important, but they need to be connected to a larger workforce architecture. In Kenya, Uthabiti’s engagement with the National Industrial Training Authority (NITA) helped to advance this agenda through the development of a recognised Childcare Worker Training Curriculum.

The work was important not simply because it could give caregivers access to a formal training pathway, but because it created an opportunity to establish a clearer occupational foundation for childcare work—one that can connect competencies, training, assessment and recognition. The curriculum had reached an important stage in that journey. The validation process was brought into the wider conversation at the 2nd Africa Childcare Forum in Mombasa in 2026, where perspectives from government, training institutions, childcare practitioners, caregivers and other stakeholders helped examine whether the emerging framework reflected the realities and needs of the workforce.

That process matters because a workforce framework should not be designed in isolation. The people who train childcare workers, employ them, regulate the sector and practise childcare every day all hold different parts of the knowledge required to make professionalisation work. Validation is therefore more than a technical step in curriculum development. It is an opportunity to build broader ownership around what childcare workers should know, what they should be able to do and how their skills should be recognised.

But curriculum validation is only one step. The longer-term question is what happens once the curriculum exists. Does it lead to recognised qualifications? Can workers access the training? Can prior experience be recognised? Does certification create pathways for progression? Do providers and employers understand and value the competencies being developed? Can government incorporate the framework into a broader workforce strategy?

These are the questions that determine whether professionalisation becomes systemic or remains a training project. The discussions at ACF therefore went beyond presenting a new curriculum. They provided an opportunity to examine, strengthen and build wider ownership of an emerging workforce framework—and to connect Kenya’s experience to the wider African conversation about how childcare professions could be developed.

In that sense, the curriculum is both a practical milestone and a starting point for a much larger conversation: what should it take to build a recognised, skilled and sustainable childcare workforce across Africa? What does a career in childcare look like? One of the clearest signs of a weak profession is the absence of a visible career pathway. For many childcare workers, the progression from entry-level care to more advanced roles is unclear.

There may be few recognised steps between being a caregiver, supervising other workers, managing a childcare setting, mentoring colleagues or becoming a trainer. This matters because professions become stronger when people can see a future within them. A young person considering childcare should be able to ask: Where can this occupation take me? What skills will I need? What qualifications are recognised?

What experience counts? What opportunities exist to specialise or take on greater responsibility? A mature workforce system should be able to provide credible answers. Career progression also changes the way experience is valued. A caregiver who has worked for ten years should not necessarily be treated in exactly the same way as someone entering the occupation for the first time. There should be mechanisms for recognising experience, assessing competence and enabling workers to build on what they already know.

This is particularly important in contexts where many experienced caregivers have entered the occupation through informal routes. Professionalisation should not mean discarding that experience. It should create pathways through which existing knowledge can be assessed, strengthened and formally recognised. Professionalisation cannot be designed without caregivers There is another dimension to workforce reform that is often overlooked: agency.

Caregivers are frequently treated as recipients of workforce programmes. They are trained, assessed and certified, while decisions about their profession are made elsewhere. That approach has limitations. Workers possess practical knowledge that cannot be fully captured in curricula or policy documents. They understand the realities of working with children and families, the constraints of different settings and the gaps between formal standards and everyday practice.

A stronger workforce system therefore needs mechanisms through which caregivers can contribute to shaping it. This is one reason caregiver networks matter. A network can provide more than peer support or access to information. It can help workers see themselves as part of a profession rather than as isolated individuals. It can create opportunities to exchange experience, identify common challenges and participate in conversations about standards, policy and working conditions.

It can also strengthen the collective visibility of a workforce that is otherwise easily overlooked. Uthabiti’s Caregiver Network has emerged from this understanding. With more than 7,300 members and growing participation, the network provides a platform through which caregivers can connect with one another and have a stronger voice in discussions about the future of their work. The point is not simply to create a larger network.

It is to help build a workforce that has agency in shaping the system in which it works. Building the institutions around the profession A profession does not exist because of workers alone. It requires institutions. Government has a central role in establishing recognition, regulation and national workforce frameworks. Training institutions need the capacity to prepare workers against credible standards.

Employers and providers need systems for recruitment, supervision and development. Professional and worker organisations need space to represent the interests of the workforce. These institutions have to connect. Otherwise, childcare workers can find themselves moving between disconnected systems: a training course that does not lead to a recognised qualification; a qualification that does not lead to better opportunities; regulation that does not reflect actual workforce realities; or employment that offers no pathway for development.

The challenge is therefore one of alignment. A national childcare workforce strategy should ideally answer several connected questions: What competencies are required? Who is responsible for developing them? How are qualifications recognised? How are workers recruited and supervised? What are the levels of progression? Who provides continuing professional development? How are experienced workers brought into the formal system?

How are workers represented? These are institutional questions, not simply training questions. And they become increasingly important as countries seek to strengthen and expand childcare provision. Professionalisation must include the people already doing the work There is a danger in designing new workforce systems around an imagined future workforce while overlooking the people already providing care.

Across Africa, childcare is already being delivered by millions of workers with different levels of experience, education and formal recognition. Any serious professionalisation strategy will have to meet this existing workforce where it is. That means creating accessible pathways into formal recognition rather than assuming that everyone can start again from the beginning. It means recognising prior learning and experience where appropriate.

It means making training accessible to workers who cannot leave their jobs for long periods. It means developing flexible progression routes. And it means ensuring that professional standards are realistic enough to be adopted while still being meaningful enough to improve practice. Professionalisation should raise standards without creating a system that excludes the very workforce it is intended to strengthen.

This is particularly important for women, who make up much of the childcare workforce. A workforce strategy that creates new qualifications but fails to create accessible pathways for existing workers risks reproducing inequality rather than addressing it. From programmes to a workforce system The shift we need is therefore from training projects to workforce systems. A project can train a cohort of caregivers.

A workforce system creates an environment in which people can enter a profession, acquire recognised skills, develop throughout their careers, receive appropriate supervision, progress into more advanced roles and participate in shaping the occupation itself. That requires coordination across institutions and over time. It also requires patience. Professionalisation is not achieved through a single curriculum, certification programme or campaign.

It is built through the gradual alignment of standards, institutions, qualifications, worker voice and government policy. This is why Uthabiti’s work on workforce development increasingly connects initiatives that might otherwise appear separate: MamaPlus and the MamaPlus Training Centre, engagement on recognised training pathways, work with government and training institutions, and the Caregiver Network. The ambition is not simply to train more people.

It is to contribute to the conditions in which childcare can become a profession. The workforce we build shapes the childcare system we get The future of childcare will ultimately be experienced through its workforce. Policies can establish standards. Financing can create possibilities. Infrastructure can expand access. But children experience childcare through the people who care for them every day.

If those workers have weak preparation, limited support and no pathway for development, the system will struggle to sustain quality. If they are recognised as professionals, supported to develop their practice, connected to meaningful career pathways and able to contribute to the institutions that shape their work, the possibilities are very different. This is why redesigning the childcare workforce is not a secondary issue within childcare reform.

It is one of the foundations on which a stronger system must be built. Africa does not simply need more childcare workers. It needs a childcare workforce that can grow with the sector, develop with the evidence, respond to changing needs and participate in shaping the future of the profession. The task ahead is therefore not to train our way out of the childcare workforce challenge.

It is to build the profession that childcare workers deserve—and that children, families and the future of Africa’s childcare systems require. This is why curriculum development and certification are important, but they need to be connected to a larger workforce architecture. In Kenya, Uthabiti’s engagement with the National Industrial Training Authority (NITA) helped to advance this agenda through the development of a recognised Childcare Worker Training Curriculum.

The significance of this work is not simply that it will provide caregivers with a formal training pathway. It is an opportunity to establish a clearer occupational foundation for childcare work—one that connects competencies, training, assessment and recognition. Just as important has been the process through which the curriculum has been developed and reviewed. Rather than treating curriculum development as a technical exercise for a single institution, Uthabiti has worked to bring different actors into the process: government and training institutions, childcare practitioners, caregivers and other stakeholders with knowledge of the realities of the workforce.

This experience has reinforced an important lesson. A childcare workforce cannot be professionalised by designing solutions for workers without involving the people and institutions who will have to use, implement, regulate and live with them. Bringing these perspectives together does more than improve a curriculum. It creates an opportunity to surface different understandings of what childcare workers actually need to know, what competencies matter in practice, what is realistic in different childcare settings and how formal training can connect with the experience of workers who are already in the profession.

The process was taken into a wider conversation at the 2nd Africa Childcare Forum in Mombasa in 2026. This created an opportunity to bring a wider group of African stakeholders into the discussion and consider the emerging framework against experience beyond Kenya. As host, Kenyan partcipants will be showcasing to the world how collective action led to the development of a comprehensive curriculum for childcare workers.

The validation is therefore not simply a technical milestone. It is part of a broader effort to build ownership around the future of the childcare profession. And that distinction matters. A curriculum can be developed. Building a profession takes much longer. It requires recognition by government, credible training institutions, accessible pathways for workers, appropriate assessment, opportunities for continuing development and, ultimately, a workforce system in which qualifications have meaning.

The ACF discussions helped move the conversation from “What should caregivers be trained to do?” to the much larger question: “What kind of professional workforce system do we need to sustain quality childcare across Africa?” and “How can Africa and the world learn from Kenya?” That is the question that professionalisation ultimately has to answer. .

title: Who Gets to Shape Africa’s Childcare Future?
author: Asayya Imaya
excerpt: The future of childcare will depend not only on what we build, but on who gets to shape what is built. When we talk about the future of childcare in Africa, we often focus on the solutions: better policies, more…
paragraphs: The future of childcare will depend not only on what we build, but on who gets to shape what is built. When we talk about the future of childcare in Africa, we often focus on the solutions: better policies, more investment, stronger services, improved training, new business models, more childcare centres and better support for families. These are all important. But beneath the question of what solutions we need is another question that receives far less attention: who gets to decide what the future of childcare should look like?

Who defines the priorities? Whose evidence is considered credible? Who decides what counts as a good childcare solution? Who determines where resources should go? Who has the opportunity to test new ideas, influence policy, build enterprises or shape the standards by which childcare is judged? These are not simply questions of participation. They are questions of power. Childcare sits at the intersection of children’s wellbeing, women’s economic participation, employment, household incomes, community life, public policy and economic development.

Because it touches so many parts of society, no single institution can hold all the knowledge or capacity required to build effective childcare systems. Yet the sector can still become concentrated around a relatively small number of organisations, institutions and funders that have historically carried much of the work. The contribution of these organisations should not be diminished.

Many have built important evidence, developed practical models, influenced policy and kept childcare on the agenda when it received little attention. But the scale and complexity of Africa’s childcare challenge raises a different question: can the future of childcare continue to depend on a relatively small group of actors? We believe it cannot. The next phase of childcare development requires not simply more activity, but a broader ecosystem of people and institutions with the opportunity, capability and agency to shape it.

The people closest to childcare have knowledge that systems often overlook Consider the caregiver. Across Africa, millions of women and men provide care for children every day, in homes, communities, childcare centres, schools and other settings. They understand the realities of caring for young children in ways that cannot be fully captured by a policy document or research report.

They know what families ask for, what children need, what makes a job difficult, what resources are missing and where systems work—or fail—in practice. Yet caregivers have often been positioned primarily as recipients of training or beneficiaries of programmes. That distinction matters. If a caregiver is understood only as someone who needs to be trained, the system asks what knowledge she lacks.

If she is understood as a professional and an actor within the childcare system, the question becomes broader: what knowledge does she possess, what conditions does she need to do her work well, what should her role be in shaping standards and policy, and what opportunities should exist for her to develop professionally and economically? The same principle applies to parents and families. Parents are not simply consumers of childcare services.

They make decisions within particular economic, cultural and social realities, often balancing affordability, trust, proximity, safety and quality. Their choices shape demand, and their experiences provide essential information about whether childcare systems are actually working. Providers, too, have knowledge that is often underused. They understand the economics of delivering care: the cost of staff, facilities, food, rent, training and compliance; the challenges of attracting and retaining workers; and the difficulty of keeping services affordable while maintaining quality.

If we want childcare markets to function better, providers cannot simply be treated as the delivery mechanism for solutions designed elsewhere. The same is true of communities, researchers, entrepreneurs, government officials, employers and investors. Each sees a different part of the system. The challenge is to bring these different forms of knowledge together. Consultation is not the same as agency There has been growing recognition across development and policy work that communities and other stakeholders should be consulted.

This is progress, but consultation alone is not enough. A person can be consulted without having meaningful influence over the decision that follows. The distinction between participation and agency is therefore important. Participation asks whether people are present. Agency asks whether they have the ability to shape what happens. For childcare, this means moving beyond asking caregivers, parents, providers and communities what they think after the main priorities have already been determined.

It means creating processes in which they can help define the problem, shape possible solutions, test them, challenge assumptions and influence decisions about what happens next. This is particularly important because childcare systems are built around relationships. The experience of a family using childcare, the experience of a caregiver providing it, the decisions of a provider, the priorities of a government and the incentives facing an investor are interconnected.

Trying to improve one part without understanding the others can produce interventions that look sensible on paper but struggle in practice. A stronger ecosystem therefore requires more than bringing different stakeholders into the same room. It requires creating structures through which they can work together over time. That is the deeper purpose of collective action. Opening the ecosystem does not mean replacing the actors already in it There is sometimes an understandable concern that calls for disruption or a more open ecosystem imply criticism of organisations that have already invested years in childcare.

That is not the argument. The work already done matters. The evidence, institutions, programmes, relationships and policy advances that exist today provide an important foundation for what comes next. The question is how to build on that foundation without reproducing a system in which too much responsibility rests with too few actors. Opening the ecosystem means creating room for more people and institutions to contribute.

It means enabling new organisations to enter the space, existing organisations to collaborate differently, governments to take stronger ownership, businesses and investors to explore appropriate opportunities, researchers to connect more directly with implementation, caregivers to organise and influence, and communities to participate in designing solutions that reflect their realities. A more open ecosystem does not necessarily mean a less coordinated one. In fact, the opposite may be true.

When responsibilities and capabilities are distributed across a wider range of actors, there is a greater need for mechanisms that connect them. Shared priorities, common evidence, professional networks, technical working groups, policy platforms and collaborative initiatives can help different actors work towards complementary objectives without requiring them to become the same organisation or follow the same model. The objective is not uniformity.

It is coherence. A healthy childcare ecosystem should be diverse enough to generate new ideas and approaches, but connected enough that knowledge, resources and learning can move between actors. Collective action requires infrastructure It is easy to talk about collaboration. It is much harder to create the conditions that make collaboration productive. People and organisations do not automatically become effective collaborators simply because they share an interest in childcare.

They need opportunities to develop trust, understand one another’s incentives, identify shared problems and work through disagreements. They need mechanisms for exchanging evidence and learning from implementation. They need places where emerging issues can be discussed before they become crises. This is why platforms for collective action matter. The Collaborative Action for Childcare, for example, is built around the idea that progress in childcare should not depend on isolated organisations pursuing separate solutions.

A collaborative platform can bring together government, practitioners, communities, researchers, private-sector actors, development partners, providers and others around shared priorities and practical action. The value of such a platform is not simply the number of organisations involved. It is the capacity it creates for those organisations to do things together that would be harder to do separately.

That could mean developing common priorities, coordinating research, strengthening workforce development, informing policy, testing solutions, sharing implementation learning or identifying pathways through which promising approaches can move towards scale. In this sense, collective action is not an event. It is an infrastructure. And building that infrastructure is part of changing the childcare system itself.

Power determines whose future gets built There is an uncomfortable reality beneath all of this: systems tend to reproduce the distribution of power that already exists within them. If decisions are consistently made by a narrow group of institutions, the resulting system will naturally reflect their perspectives, incentives and assumptions. Even where those actors are well intentioned, important perspectives can remain outside the room.

Opening the childcare ecosystem is therefore partly about changing the distribution of influence. Who has access to information? Who has relationships with policymakers? Who can mobilise resources? Who gets to define quality? Who can introduce new ideas? Who is trusted as an expert? Who gets to lead? Who receives recognition when progress is made? These questions matter because childcare is entering a period in which its importance is increasingly being recognised across multiple sectors.

As investment grows and new actors enter the space, there is an opportunity to shape a more inclusive ecosystem from the outset. That does not mean every actor should have equal responsibility or equal influence in every decision. Governments have particular responsibilities. Professionals have particular expertise. Communities have particular knowledge. Researchers have particular roles.

Investors have particular capabilities. The point is not to erase these differences. The point is to ensure that the system is capable of drawing on them. From beneficiaries to builders One of the most important shifts Africa's childcare sector can make is to stop seeing people only as beneficiaries of systems and start recognising them as builders of those systems. Caregivers can be organisers, professionals, trainers, advocates and leaders.

Parents can influence service design and policy. Providers can contribute to market development and quality improvement. Entrepreneurs can develop new models and services. Researchers can become partners in implementation rather than observers of it. Communities can shape locally appropriate approaches. Governments can create the institutional conditions for all of these actors to contribute.

This is not a romantic view of participation. It requires investment in capability. People need information, skills, networks, resources and institutions through which they can exercise agency. Organisations need stronger capacity to collaborate. Governments need the technical and institutional capability to coordinate complex systems. Workers need professional structures through which their interests and expertise can be represented.

In other words, opening the ecosystem is not simply about inviting more people in. It is about making it possible for them to contribute meaningfully once they are there. This is where the idea of disruption becomes important. Disruption is not about replacing one set of powerful actors with another. It is about changing the underlying pattern so that the childcare ecosystem becomes less dependent on a few organisations and more capable of generating leadership from many places.

Africa does not need one childcare champion The scale of Africa’s childcare challenge makes the idea of a single organisation carrying the solution increasingly unrealistic. What Africa needs instead is an ecosystem of capable actors that can contribute different forms of expertise, capital, innovation and leadership. That will require organisations willing to share knowledge rather than protect it, governments willing to work beyond institutional boundaries, funders willing to invest in ecosystem capacity as well as individual projects, researchers willing to engage with implementation, businesses willing to explore the economic dimensions of care, and practitioners willing to learn across contexts.

It will also require a different understanding of leadership. Leadership in a complex system is not always about being the organisation at the centre. Sometimes it is about creating the conditions for others to lead. It is about building platforms, connecting people, making knowledge accessible, convening difficult conversations and helping ideas move between institutions. That kind of leadership can be less visible than running a large programme.

But it can have a much wider effect. For Uthabiti Africa, this is an important part of the work. The ambition is not to become the organisation that owns Africa’s childcare agenda. It is to help create an ecosystem in which more actors can shape that agenda, contribute solutions and take responsibility for what happens next. The measure of success, therefore, is not how central Uthabiti becomes.

It is how much stronger the ecosystem becomes. The future should be shaped by the ecosystem that will build it Africa’s childcare future is too important to be designed by a narrow group of institutions, however capable or committed they may be. The question is not whether the organisations that have carried the work to date should continue to lead. They should. The question is whether leadership can become more distributed, whether more actors can develop the capability to contribute, and whether the systems connecting them can become stronger.

That is what opening the childcare ecosystem should mean. It means moving from consultation to co-creation, from beneficiaries to builders, from isolated programmes to connected systems, and from a small number of organisations carrying the agenda to a much broader community capable of shaping it. The childcare systems Africa needs will not emerge from one institution having the perfect answer.

They will emerge from many actors bringing different forms of knowledge, capability and agency together—and having the structures to turn those contributions into collective progress. The future of childcare should therefore not simply be something that is delivered to Africa, or even something designed for Africa. It should be something built by the people, institutions and communities that will live and work within it.

The question is no longer only what should Africa’s childcare system look like? It is also: Who gets to shape it? The conversations surrounding ACFMombasa2026 formed part of this wider effort to consider how that future could be shaped. The challenge now is to ensure that the principles of collective action, inclusion and shared ownership continue to inform the decisions, partnerships and investments that follow.

Because the work does not end when a forum concludes. It continues in the institutions we strengthen, the voices we include, the relationships we build and the decisions we make together. The question is no longer only what should Africa’s childcare system look like? It is also: who gets to shape it?

title: Can Childcare Become a Functioning Market Without Losing Its Social Purpose?
author: Asayya Imaya
excerpt: The question is not whether childcare should be a market. It already is. The question is what kind of market we choose to build. There is an understandable discomfort when the language of markets enters a conversation…
paragraphs: The question is not whether childcare should be a market. It already is. The question is what kind of market we choose to build. There is an understandable discomfort when the language of markets enters a conversation about childcare. Childcare is about children. It is about safety, development, relationships, learning and the wellbeing of families. It is also deeply connected to questions of equality and women's economic participation.

For many people, describing childcare as a “market” can sound as though something fundamentally human is being reduced to a commercial transaction. That concern deserves to be taken seriously. But there is another uncomfortable reality: childcare is already an economic activity. Across Africa, families pay for care. Caregivers earn livelihoods. Individuals and organisations operate childcare services.

Governments spend public resources on early childhood programmes and infrastructure. Training institutions prepare workers. Businesses supply food, equipment, furniture, learning materials and other services. Financial institutions provide—or could provide—capital. Employers increasingly confront the implications of childcare for their workforce. The question, therefore, is not whether childcare should become a market.

In many respects, it already is one. The more important question is whether the childcare market is functioning well enough to deliver what children, families, workers and the wider economy need. In much of Africa, the answer is no. The market is fragmented, heavily informal and uneven in quality. Providers often operate under significant financial pressure. Families have limited information and highly unequal purchasing power.

Caregivers can work for low wages without recognised career pathways. Access to finance is difficult for many providers. Regulation may be either insufficiently enforced or difficult for small providers to navigate. Public investment is often inadequate to meet the scale of demand. These are not arguments against markets. They are arguments for building a better market system. The danger of confusing markets with commercialisation The first distinction we need to make is between a market and commercialisation.

Commercialisation suggests that the primary objective is financial return: identify a paying customer, sell a service and maximise revenue. That approach may work for some products and services, but childcare cannot be understood in those terms alone. A childcare service is not simply a product purchased by a consumer. Its quality has consequences for someone who is not the person making the purchasing decision—the child.

The ability to pay is also highly unequal, while the benefits of childcare extend beyond the individual family to employers, communities and economies. This creates a set of social and economic considerations that cannot be left entirely to market forces. A functioning childcare market therefore needs rules and institutions that protect children, support quality and promote inclusion.

It needs regulation, public policy, standards and accountability. In some contexts, it may require public financing or subsidies because the market price that a low-income family can afford will not necessarily cover the cost of quality care. This is not a failure of the market. It is a recognition that markets operate within societies and institutions. The real mistake would be to assume that because childcare has a social purpose, its economic foundations do not matter.

They matter enormously. A provider that cannot cover its costs will struggle to retain qualified caregivers. A caregiver who cannot earn a sustainable income will struggle to remain in the profession. A training institution that cannot connect its graduates to employment will struggle to create meaningful workforce pathways. A provider that cannot access finance cannot easily improve infrastructure.

A family that cannot afford care cannot benefit from a service that exists only on paper. The social purpose of childcare depends, in part, on the strength of the economic system around it. The childcare market already has participants—but they do not operate as one system Look closely at the childcare landscape and it becomes clear that there is no absence of economic activity. There are childcare providers serving families in formal centres, homes, communities and other settings.

There are caregivers earning incomes from their work. There are people establishing childcare businesses because they see demand in their communities. There are training providers developing skills. There are suppliers responding to the needs of childcare centres. There are employers trying to understand how childcare affects their workforce. What is often missing is the connective tissue between these actors.

A caregiver may complete training without having a recognised qualification that improves her employment prospects. A provider may have a waiting list of families but lack the financing or management systems required to expand. A financial institution may see childcare businesses as too small or informal to finance. A family may want quality care but lack reliable information about which providers offer it.

A government may have established standards but lack the mechanisms and resources to support providers in meeting them. Each part of the system exists, but the relationships between them are weak. This is one reason why simply increasing the number of childcare programmes or providers does not necessarily produce a stronger childcare sector. Markets function through relationships. Workers need employers.

Providers need families. Businesses need customers. Investors need viable enterprises. Regulators need information from the sector they regulate. Training institutions need to understand what employers require. Families need information about services. Government needs capable institutions and partners to implement policy. Strengthening these relationships is therefore as important as creating individual interventions.

This is the essence of a market-systems perspective: rather than asking only whether a particular service exists, we ask what prevents the wider system from functioning effectively and inclusively. The economics of the provider cannot be ignored Perhaps nowhere is this more important than at the level of the childcare provider. We often discuss quality as though it were simply a question of training and standards.

But quality has an economics. A provider needs enough revenue to pay workers. Facilities need to be safe and maintained. Children need appropriate food, materials and equipment. Workers need manageable workloads. Providers need systems for administration and safeguarding. In some settings, they need to comply with regulatory requirements that carry costs. If families cannot afford higher fees, the provider has limited room to increase revenue.

If the provider cannot increase revenue, there may be little room to increase wages or invest in quality. This creates a difficult equation. We can tell providers to improve quality, but if the economics of provision make improvement financially impossible, the instruction will not be enough. This is why building a stronger childcare market requires attention to the business realities of provision without reducing providers to businesses alone.

There is a need to understand which models can become financially viable, which require public support, which can benefit from cooperative approaches, and where different forms of finance might be appropriate. There is also a need to explore whether providers can achieve efficiencies through shared services, networks, technology, procurement or other forms of collaboration. The answer will not be the same everywhere.

An urban childcare centre serving working families may have a different economic model from a community-based provider in a lower-income rural setting. A workplace childcare service may operate differently from a private centre. Public provision will have different financing dynamics from household-funded provision. A functioning market system does not mean forcing every provider into one model.

It means creating the conditions in which different models can emerge, improve and serve different needs. Better markets can create better jobs The workforce is another reason the economics of childcare matter. Care work has historically been undervalued partly because it has been associated with women's unpaid domestic labour. That legacy continues to shape the paid childcare workforce, where many workers remain poorly paid and have limited opportunities for professional progression.

This is not simply a labour issue. It is a market issue. If the market places little value on childcare skills, there is limited incentive for workers to invest in those skills. If qualifications do not translate into better employment opportunities, training becomes disconnected from career development. If providers cannot afford better wages, workers remain trapped in low-value employment.

And if families cannot afford services, providers have limited ability to improve the employment conditions of their staff. The cycle has to be broken at multiple points. This is why workforce professionalisation cannot be treated as a training intervention alone. It needs recognised qualifications, employer demand, credible career pathways, better working conditions and an economic model that allows providers to reward skills.

Work such as Uthabiti's MamaPlus initiative and its engagement around childcare workforce development illustrates this broader principle. The objective is not simply to put more caregivers through courses. It is to contribute to a childcare workforce system in which training, professional recognition, employment and economic opportunity are connected. That distinction is important.

Training people for a weak market does not transform the market. A stronger market has to create greater value for the skills that workers acquire. The role of government is not diminished by a market approach One of the concerns about talking about childcare as a market is that it can imply that government should step aside. The opposite is true. Government has a critical role in creating the conditions under which the childcare system can function.

It sets policy and regulatory frameworks, establishes standards, invests public resources, provides or enables infrastructure, protects children and workers, and can influence how different actors participate in the sector. In many African countries, the state will also remain essential to addressing the affordability gap. If childcare is left entirely to household purchasing power, quality provision may become accessible primarily to families who can afford it.

A market-systems approach therefore asks government to do something more sophisticated than either providing everything itself or leaving everything to the private sector. It asks: What functions should government perform, what should other actors provide, and what conditions need to exist for the system as a whole to work? This can open space for productive collaboration. Public institutions might provide infrastructure while private or community providers deliver services.

Government might establish qualifications and standards while training institutions develop the workforce. Public resources might be used to catalyse provision in underserved areas. Financial institutions might develop products suited to childcare providers. Employers might contribute to solutions because they benefit from a more reliable workforce. The appropriate balance will differ across countries and contexts.

But the principle remains: government is not replaced by markets. Government helps shape the market. What would an inclusive childcare market look like? If we are serious about market development, we need to define success carefully. It cannot simply mean more businesses making money from childcare. A successful childcare market system would allow providers to operate sustainably while maintaining strong standards for children's wellbeing.

It would create meaningful employment and career opportunities for childcare workers. It would give families greater access to reliable, affordable and appropriate services. It would create opportunities for entrepreneurs and businesses to innovate. It would attract investment where investment is appropriate. And it would ensure that the benefits of market development are not restricted to households with the highest purchasing power.

That last point is critical. A market can grow and still fail society. If investment flows only towards affluent neighbourhoods, the number of childcare businesses may increase while inequality in access becomes worse. If providers compete primarily on price, quality may suffer. If regulation becomes so burdensome that small providers cannot formalise, informality may deepen rather than diminish.

The objective, therefore, is not simply market growth. It is market development that serves a social purpose. That requires deliberate attention to inclusion, quality, affordability and children's rights alongside financial sustainability. It also requires experimentation. Different financing mechanisms may need to be tested. Different provider models may need to emerge. Workforce systems will need to evolve.

Governments will need to learn what forms of regulation and public investment produce the strongest results. There will not be one universal model. Africa's childcare markets will develop differently because African economies, households, labour markets and public institutions are different. The task is to build systems that can learn and adapt. From isolated programmes to market-building This is where the work of organisations such as Uthabiti Africa becomes particularly relevant.

If the problem were simply a shortage of childcare centres, the solution might be to build more centres. If the problem were simply a shortage of trained caregivers, the answer might be to train more caregivers. But the constraints are interconnected. A new centre does not solve a workforce problem if there is no professional pathway for caregivers. Training does not solve a provider problem if employers cannot afford qualified workers.

Finance does not solve an access problem if services remain unaffordable to families. Policy does not produce change if institutions lack the capacity to implement it. The work therefore has to extend beyond individual interventions towards the relationships and conditions that connect them. This is why collective platforms such as Collaborative Action for Childcare (CAC) matter. Building a functioning childcare market system requires actors who do not traditionally sit at the same table to understand one another's roles and constraints.

Government, providers, caregivers, researchers, businesses, investors, families and development partners each control different pieces of the system. No single organisation can assemble all of those pieces. The role of a systems and market-systems organisation is therefore not to become the childcare market itself. It is to help create the conditions in which the market can become stronger, more inclusive and more capable of delivering social value.
