That can mean generating evidence, convening actors, testing approaches, strengthening institutions, supporting workforce pathways, helping government engage with the sector and creating platforms through which learning can spread. It is fundamentally about building capacity beyond the organisation itself. The market should serve the purpose—not redefine it There is a final principle that should remain non-negotiable.

Childcare is not valuable because it can generate revenue. It is valuable because children need care, families need support and economies depend on people being able to participate in productive life. Economic sustainability is a means of strengthening that system, not the purpose that replaces it. The challenge is to hold both truths at once. We need childcare services that are financially viable, because financially fragile services are difficult to sustain.

We need childcare workers who can earn decent livelihoods, because a professional workforce is essential to quality. We need providers who can grow and innovate, because the scale of the need demands more capacity. We need investment, because public resources alone will not necessarily meet every need. And we need markets that can respond to demand and create new opportunities. But we also need regulation, public leadership, accountability and deliberate attention to equity because childcare is not an ordinary commodity.

The question is therefore not whether childcare should be commercialised. It is whether we can build an economic system around childcare without allowing the economics to displace its social purpose. That is a harder challenge—and a much more worthwhile one. Africa has an opportunity to move beyond the false choice between childcare as a social good and childcare as an economic sector.

It can build a system in which the two reinforce one another: where better economic conditions make better care possible, and better care creates wider economic opportunity. The goal should not be a childcare market at any cost. It should be a functioning, inclusive childcare market system that works for children, families, workers, providers, governments and the economies they sustain.
That is the market worth building.

title: Why Good Childcare Innovations Don’t Scale
author: Asayya Imaya
excerpt: Moving from promising pilots to systems that can work at scale Africa does not have a shortage of ideas for improving childcare. Across the continent, organisations, governments, communities, researchers and…
paragraphs: Moving from promising pilots to systems that can work at scale Africa does not have a shortage of ideas for improving childcare. Across the continent, organisations, governments, communities, researchers and entrepreneurs are developing new approaches to early childhood care, caregiver training, provider support, parental engagement, financing and service delivery. Some of these innovations are producing encouraging results.

They demonstrate that childcare can be delivered differently, that caregivers can be better supported, that providers can become more capable and that families can access better services. And yet, many promising approaches struggle to move beyond the place where they were first developed. A pilot works in one community, but cannot be sustained when external funding ends. A training model produces strong results with a small group of caregivers, but cannot be absorbed into national workforce systems.

A provider model succeeds with intensive technical support, but becomes financially difficult when that support is removed. A policy is adopted, but implementation remains limited. An innovation attracts attention, but not the financing, institutional ownership or market conditions required to reach thousands or millions of people. This creates a recurring pattern in development: we become very good at proving that something can work, but much less successful at changing the conditions that would allow it to work at scale.

Childcare exposes this problem particularly clearly. The question is not simply whether a better model can be designed. The more difficult question is whether the system around that model is capable of adopting, financing, regulating, delivering and continuously improving it. That is where scale is won or lost. The pilot is often the easiest part There is a reason pilots are attractive.

A pilot creates a manageable environment in which an organisation can concentrate resources, work closely with participants, solve problems quickly and make adjustments as it learns. A strong team can provide technical assistance. A funder can cover costs that would otherwise be difficult to meet. Participants can receive intensive support. The programme can operate with a degree of flexibility that is often impossible within large public systems or fragmented markets.

Under those conditions, good results are possible. But success under pilot conditions does not automatically tell us whether the model can survive outside them. Consider a childcare workforce programme. A pilot might provide caregivers with high-quality training, mentoring, materials and ongoing supervision. Participants may demonstrate significant improvements. But what happens when thousands more caregivers need the same support?

Who pays for the training? Who certifies it? Which institution recognises the qualification? Who employs the workers? How will continuing professional development be financed? Can the approach fit within existing government systems? The pilot may have solved the training problem. It may not have solved the workforce-system problem. The same applies to childcare providers. A programme might help a group of providers improve their business practices, strengthen safeguarding and enhance quality.

But if the providers still cannot access finance, if families cannot afford quality services, if regulation is unclear or if the local market cannot sustain the model, the intervention may remain dependent on external support. This is why the question “Does it work?” is only the beginning. The more important questions are: Why does it work? What conditions make it possible? Which of those conditions exist elsewhere?

Which need to be created? And who will own the work when the original organisation steps back? Those are the questions that turn an innovation into a pathway towards scale. Scale is not replication One of the most persistent assumptions in development is that if a model works in one place, the next step is to reproduce it in many others. But childcare rarely works that way. A childcare model developed in Nairobi may contain valuable principles that can inform work in Kampala, Accra or another African city, but the institutional, economic and cultural environment will be different.

The structure of government may differ. The childcare workforce may have different qualifications. Household incomes and patterns of employment may differ. Regulatory systems may operate differently. Providers may have different business models. Families may have different expectations. Simply copying the original model can therefore produce disappointing results. Scaling should be understood less as replication and more as adaptation within a system.

The objective is to understand which elements of an innovation are fundamental to its effectiveness and which can—and should—change according to context. This is particularly important for Africa because the continent is not a single childcare market or policy environment. There are significant differences between countries, and equally significant differences within them. Urban and rural childcare systems face different pressures.

Formal and informal providers operate under different conditions. Public provision and private provision have different constraints. A serious approach to scale therefore has to allow local actors to shape what happens next. The knowledge generated in one setting should travel. The model itself does not necessarily need to. This distinction becomes even more important when considering who owns the innovation.

If a programme can only be delivered effectively by the organisation that originally created it, then its potential for genuine systems change is limited. The ultimate test is whether other institutions can understand it, adapt it, finance it and make it their own. Scale happens when ownership expands. The missing ingredient is often the system around the innovation Many innovations fail to scale not because the idea is weak, but because the surrounding system has not changed.

Imagine a childcare training programme that successfully prepares caregivers for a new professional qualification. If there is no recognised occupational pathway, the qualification may have little value in the labour market. If providers cannot afford to employ better-qualified caregivers, the training may not translate into better jobs. If government does not recognise the qualification, it may remain outside the formal workforce system.

The training itself may be excellent. The system simply has nowhere to put it. This is why systems change requires attention to the relationships between institutions and actors. For childcare, those relationships include government and providers, training institutions and employers, families and providers, workers and employers, financiers and enterprises, researchers and policymakers.

An intervention that changes only one part of this network may produce a strong local result without changing the conditions that determine whether that result can spread. The challenge is therefore to identify the systemic constraints behind the problem. Sometimes the constraint is finance. Sometimes it is regulation. Sometimes it is workforce capacity. Sometimes it is weak demand or limited purchasing power.

Sometimes it is a lack of information. Sometimes it is fragmented leadership. Often it is several of these at once. This changes the role of innovation. An innovation should not only demonstrate a better way of doing something. It should help us understand what needs to change around it. That knowledge can be more valuable than the model itself. Financing determines what survives One of the clearest barriers to scale is financing.

Many childcare innovations begin with grant funding because grant funding allows organisations to experiment. This is often appropriate at the early stage. But an innovation that depends indefinitely on grants has not necessarily found a sustainable pathway to scale. The problem is not that grants are inherently unsustainable. Development finance can play an important role in testing new approaches, absorbing early risk and generating evidence.

The problem arises when temporary funding becomes the permanent economic model. A childcare workforce programme, for example, may be highly effective when donor resources cover training, supervision and coordination. But if the long-term system has no mechanism for financing those functions, the programme may shrink when the grant ends. Similarly, a provider-support initiative may demonstrate that better business practices improve quality and sustainability.

But if providers have no access to appropriate finance, or families cannot afford the resulting service, there may be no viable route to expansion. This is why scaling requires a financing strategy from relatively early in the development process. Who ultimately pays? Government? Families? Employers? Providers? Investors? Development partners? Some combination of these? The answer will vary according to the intervention.

But asking the question early forces innovators to think beyond the pilot. It also opens the possibility of using different forms of capital for different stages of development. Grant funding may support experimentation. Catalytic finance may help demonstrate new models. Public resources may support services with strong social benefits but limited commercial returns. Private investment may be appropriate for enterprises capable of generating sustainable revenues.

A mature childcare ecosystem will need more than one financing mechanism. Government ownership is essential—but ownership does not mean government does everything Another common reason promising innovations struggle to scale is that government is brought in too late. A programme may be designed, implemented and evaluated for several years before government is approached about adoption.

By that point, the model may have been built around processes, staffing structures and funding arrangements that do not fit within public systems. The result is predictable: government may appreciate the innovation but struggle to absorb it. A better approach is to engage public institutions earlier—not simply as eventual funders, but as partners in understanding the problem and designing the pathway to scale.

Government has responsibilities that cannot be delegated to projects. It sets policy, establishes regulatory frameworks, develops public systems, allocates resources and ultimately has a central role in ensuring that children and families can access essential services. But government ownership does not mean government has to deliver every component itself. The stronger question is what each actor is best placed to do.

A government may establish standards and qualifications while training institutions deliver programmes. Providers may operate services while government provides infrastructure or targeted financing. Private businesses may develop innovations within a policy framework. Civil society organisations may generate evidence and support implementation. Communities may help adapt approaches to local realities.

This is not a question of choosing between public and private provision. It is about building a system in which different actors can perform complementary functions. When this happens, scaling becomes less about government adopting an NGO programme and more about institutions collectively building a solution that can endure. The workforce is often the hidden constraint There is another issue that deserves greater attention: scale requires people.

A model may be technically sound, but if there are not enough appropriately skilled people to implement it, expansion will eventually stall. This is particularly significant in childcare because the workforce is at the centre of service delivery. Expanding access without strengthening the workforce can produce a larger system without a stronger one. Professionalisation therefore has to be part of the scaling conversation from the beginning.

That means considering qualifications, accreditation, career progression, remuneration, working conditions, supervision and ongoing learning. It also means asking whether training institutions have the capacity to produce workers at the scale required and whether employers have the economic capacity to absorb them. Uthabiti's work through MamaPlus and the MamaPlus Training Centre provides one example of approaching workforce development as a system rather than simply a series of training courses.

Engagement with government institutions and efforts to strengthen recognised childcare qualifications are important precisely because they connect individual skills development to a wider workforce architecture. The same principle applies to providers. If childcare businesses and community providers are expected to expand access, they need the management, financing, infrastructure and support systems required to operate sustainably.

Scaling services without strengthening the organisations responsible for delivering them simply transfers pressure from one part of the system to another. Evidence should help systems learn, not simply prove that a project worked There is also a problem with how we think about evidence. Too often, evaluation is designed primarily to answer whether a programme succeeded according to its original objectives.

That is important, but it does not tell us everything we need to know about scale. A more useful body of evidence asks what happened, why it happened, under what conditions it happened and what would need to change for the result to be achieved elsewhere. It asks what participants changed, what providers changed, what institutions changed and what remained resistant. It examines costs as well as outcomes.

It identifies unintended consequences. It pays attention to implementation. And it asks what the experience tells us about the wider system. This kind of evidence is particularly valuable for collective action because it gives different actors a common basis for deciding what to do next. That is one of the functions of platforms such as Collaborative Action for Childcare (CAC). Bringing actors together around shared priorities creates the possibility of moving beyond isolated learning towards collective learning.

A successful innovation should not remain the property of the organisation that developed it. Its lessons should become available to the wider ecosystem. This is how knowledge begins to travel. The real measure of scale is what remains when the programme leaves Perhaps the most useful test of an innovation is also the simplest: What remains when the original programme is no longer there?

If the answer is “not much,” then we may have achieved a successful project rather than systems change. But if the intervention has contributed to stronger institutions, recognised qualifications, viable provider models, better policy, new financing mechanisms, improved information, stronger professional networks or new relationships between actors, then something more important has happened. The system has changed its capacity.

This is a different understanding of sustainability. Sustainability is not simply whether a programme can continue operating after donor funding ends. It is whether the functions created or strengthened by the programme can continue within the wider ecosystem. That may mean another organisation takes over. It may mean government incorporates a model into an existing system. It may mean a market emerges around a service.

It may mean a professional association sustains a workforce network. It may mean providers become capable of financing their own improvements. In each case, the original intervention becomes less important than the capability it helped create. That is the point at which an innovation begins to move from project to system. Building pathways to scale requires a different kind of organisation This has implications for organisations working in childcare.

If the goal is systems change, success cannot be measured only by the number of people directly reached by an organisation's programmes. Direct reach matters, but it is only one measure. We also need to ask how an organisation is changing the conditions around the problem. Is it strengthening government capacity? Is it helping establish professional pathways? Is it improving the economics of provision?

Is it generating evidence that others can use? Is it creating platforms for collective action? Is it enabling other organisations to adopt and adapt successful approaches? Is it making itself less central over time by strengthening the capacity of the wider ecosystem? These are harder questions to answer than counting programme participants. But they are closer to the real work of systems change.

For Uthabiti Africa, this is an important part of the organisation's role. The ambition is not to develop childcare models that remain permanently dependent on Uthabiti. It is to contribute to the conditions in which governments, providers, workers, businesses, researchers and other organisations can take solutions forward. That is why convening, evidence, workforce development, policy engagement and practical demonstration all matter.

They are not separate activities. They are different ways of strengthening the ecosystem around childcare. From innovation to infrastructure The childcare sector needs innovation. But it needs something more difficult than innovation alone. It needs infrastructure for innovation to travel. That includes institutions capable of adoption, financing mechanisms capable of sustaining growth, policies capable of creating enabling conditions, workforce systems capable of producing skilled professionals, markets capable of supporting viable providers, and networks capable of sharing knowledge.

Without these foundations, we will continue to see the same cycle: a promising idea emerges, a pilot demonstrates results, attention grows, funding follows for a period, and then the initiative struggles to move beyond its original boundaries. The answer is not to stop piloting. We need experimentation. But every experiment should be connected to a larger question: what would have to change for this to become part of the way childcare is normally done?

That question forces us to think about scale from the beginning. It forces innovators to engage government earlier, understand provider economics, consider workforce implications, identify financing pathways, generate evidence that others can use and create models that other actors can adapt. Most importantly, it changes the definition of success. The goal is not for one organisation to become very good at delivering one solution.

The goal is for the childcare ecosystem to become better at solving problems. That is the difference between scaling a programme and changing a system. Africa does not need another generation of childcare pilots that demonstrate what is possible but leave the underlying conditions unchanged. It needs innovations that become learning, learning that becomes institutional capacity, institutional capacity that creates stronger markets and public systems, and those systems that can continue improving long after the original innovation has moved on.

The real test of a childcare innovation is not whether it can work once. It is whether it can help create a system in which better childcare can keep working, growing and adapting without depending on the organisation that started it. That is what scale should mean.

title: Building African Childcare Systems, Not Importing Models
author: Asayya Imaya
excerpt: What would an African childcare ecosystem look like if we built it from our own realities? Africa does not have a shortage of childcare ideas. What it lacks is something more fundamental: childcare systems that are…
paragraphs: What would an African childcare ecosystem look like if we built it from our own realities? Africa does not have a shortage of childcare ideas. What it lacks is something more fundamental: childcare systems that are consistently financed, appropriately regulated, adequately staffed, economically viable and capable of adapting to the realities of the families and communities they serve.

For decades, childcare development across the continent has often been influenced by models, frameworks and approaches developed elsewhere. There is nothing inherently wrong with learning from international experience. No country develops in isolation, and Africa has much to gain from global research, practice and evidence. The problem begins when learning becomes replication. A model developed in one economic, cultural or institutional context can be transferred to another with the assumption that the same intervention will produce the same result.

When that happens, local realities can become an afterthought rather than the starting point for design. But African childcare systems cannot be built successfully by importing solutions and expecting contexts to adapt themselves around them. They have to be built from the realities of African families, economies, institutions, communities and labour markets. That does not mean rejecting international evidence.

It means engaging with it critically, adapting what is useful, discarding what is not, and generating new knowledge from African experience. The question is not whether Africa should learn from the world. It is whether Africa is also prepared to recognise that the world has much to learn from Africa. There is no single African childcare system The first thing to acknowledge is that “Africa” is not a childcare context.

The continent contains enormously different economic, political, demographic and social realities. The childcare needs of a rapidly growing city are not identical to those of a rural community. The challenges facing a low-income household are not the same as those facing a professional family with access to formal childcare. Public institutions have different capacities across countries and regions.

Labour markets differ. Cultural expectations around family and care differ. The role of grandparents and extended families differs. Patterns of migration, urbanisation and informal employment differ. Even within the same country, childcare systems can look radically different from one community to another. This diversity is not a problem to be solved. It is a reality that good systems design must accommodate.

An African approach to childcare should therefore not mean developing one continental model and asking every country to reproduce it. It should mean building a shared capacity to develop, test, adapt and scale solutions in ways that make sense locally. That distinction is critical. A strong childcare ecosystem should have enough common ground to allow countries and actors to learn from one another, but enough flexibility to allow local systems to evolve according to their own circumstances.

The goal is not uniformity. It is interconnected capacity. Start with the systems families already use Building better childcare does not mean starting from zero. Families across Africa have always developed ways of caring for children. Grandparents, relatives, neighbours and community networks often play essential roles. Women in particular have historically absorbed enormous amounts of unpaid care within households.

Informal childcare providers serve families in places where formal services may be unavailable or unaffordable. These arrangements are sometimes described simply as evidence of a gap that formal systems need to fill. That is too simplistic. They are also sources of knowledge about how childcare actually works in communities. They tell us about the importance of proximity, trust, flexibility, affordability and social relationships.

They show how families cope when formal services do not match the realities of their working lives. They also reveal where informal systems place unsustainable burdens on women or leave children and workers without adequate protection. A stronger childcare system should therefore neither romanticise informal care nor dismiss it. It should ask what can be learned from it, what needs to be strengthened, what needs to change and where formal institutions can add value.

This is especially important in African economies where a significant proportion of workers earn livelihoods outside formal employment. A childcare system designed around the assumption that every parent works predictable hours for a formal employer will inevitably exclude many of the families it is intended to serve. The same is true of provider models. A system built entirely around large formal centres may not be the most appropriate or affordable solution in every community.

Smaller providers, community-based models, home-based care and other forms of provision may all have a role, provided that children are protected and quality standards are meaningful and achievable. The task is to build a system that reflects how people actually live and work—not one that assumes they live and work differently. Local ownership is not a slogan There is a tendency in development conversations to speak about “local ownership” as though it simply means involving local stakeholders in implementation.

True ownership goes further. It means that local institutions have the authority, capability and resources to make decisions about what happens in their systems. A childcare policy should not remain dependent on an external organisation to interpret or implement it. A workforce system should be capable of being sustained by national institutions. Providers should be able to adapt approaches to their markets.

Researchers and practitioners should be generating knowledge that influences local policy. Communities should have mechanisms through which their experience can shape services. This is one reason government matters so much. Government is not simply another stakeholder in a childcare ecosystem. It has a distinctive responsibility for creating the policy, regulatory and institutional environment within which childcare operates.

But government ownership does not mean centralising every decision. Effective systems create room for local governments, communities, providers, workers and other actors to contribute. They establish common standards and public objectives while allowing implementation to respond to context. This balance between national direction and local adaptation is likely to be particularly important as African countries seek to strengthen childcare systems.

A national policy can establish ambition. It cannot, by itself, determine what works in every neighbourhood. That requires institutions and actors who are close enough to the ground to understand implementation and capable enough to feed what they learn back into the wider system. African learning should move in more than one direction If childcare systems are to become stronger across the continent, Africa needs more than individual country programmes.

It needs African learning infrastructure. There is enormous value in being able to learn from what another African country has tried—not because its approach can simply be copied, but because it can reveal possibilities, risks and questions that may otherwise take years to discover. A workforce qualification developed in one country may provide useful lessons for another. A financing mechanism tested in one city may generate ideas for providers elsewhere.

A government may learn from another government's approach to regulation. A community-based model may offer insights into how trust and affordability can be strengthened in a different setting. But this requires more than occasional conferences. It requires relationships between institutions, practitioners, policymakers, researchers and other actors that allow knowledge to move continuously.

It also requires a willingness to share failure. Development systems often celebrate successful innovations while quietly abandoning unsuccessful ones. Yet for countries trying to build new systems, understanding what did not work can be just as valuable as understanding what did. If one childcare financing model failed because providers could not meet its requirements, that lesson should be available to others before they repeat the experiment.

If a training approach could not be absorbed into government structures, that experience should inform future workforce design. If a regulatory framework unintentionally pushed small providers further into informality, others should be able to learn from it. Learning becomes powerful when it travels. That is one of the reasons continental platforms matter. The Africa Childcare Forum, for example, was more than an event at which people exchanged presentations.

It contributed to a wider infrastructure for African childcare learning—connecting evidence, policy, practice and relationships across countries and helping actors see their work as part of a larger continental conversation. The ambition should be to create a community of practice that continues working long after people leave the conference room. Systems need to be built around people, not programmes One of the biggest differences between a programme and a system is what happens when the programme ends.

A programme has defined activities, participants, timelines and funding. A system has institutions, relationships, incentives and capabilities that continue to operate. This distinction matters because childcare is too important to remain dependent on short-term projects. A training programme may help caregivers acquire new skills. But the larger question is whether a country has a workforce system that recognises those skills and creates pathways for employment and progression.

A provider-support programme may help centres improve their operations. But the larger question is whether providers have access to the finance, information, infrastructure and market conditions needed to remain viable. A policy initiative may generate a new framework. But the larger question is whether institutions have the capacity and resources to implement it. A successful pilot may demonstrate that something is possible.

But the larger question is whether the surrounding ecosystem is capable of taking it forward. This is why systems-building requires a different kind of investment. It requires investing in institutions as well as interventions. It requires strengthening relationships as well as delivering activities. It requires building local capability rather than creating permanent dependence on external expertise.

And it requires accepting that some of the most important results may be less visible than the launch of a new programme: a government department becoming more capable, a professional network becoming stronger, a qualification becoming recognised, providers becoming financially viable, or different actors beginning to coordinate around shared priorities. These are the foundations on which durable systems are built. The economics of African childcare must be part of the design A locally grounded childcare system must also reflect the realities of African economies.

Childcare cannot be designed separately from household incomes, employment patterns, urbanisation, women's economic participation and the large informal economy. A service that is technically excellent but unaffordable to most families will not create broad access. A workforce model that assumes high salaries but provides no viable way for providers to finance those salaries will not survive.

A provider model that depends on stable monthly fees may struggle in communities where household incomes fluctuate. A financing mechanism designed for large formal enterprises may be irrelevant to small childcare providers. These are not secondary implementation issues. They determine whether the system can function. This is where a market-systems perspective becomes particularly useful.

It encourages us to examine the incentives and relationships that shape behaviour across the sector. What makes a provider invest in quality? What allows a caregiver to invest in professional development? What enables families to afford reliable care? What would make financial institutions willing to serve childcare enterprises? Where does public financing have the greatest effect? The answers will vary across countries.

But asking the questions allows childcare to be designed around the economic realities of the people who depend on it. That is especially important if childcare is to contribute to women's economic participation. A childcare system that enables women to enter paid work but requires them to spend a disproportionate share of their income on care has not fully solved the problem. Affordability, accessibility and quality have to be considered together.

The continent needs more than childcare programmes; it needs childcare ecosystems This is ultimately the larger shift. A programme asks what intervention can address a particular problem. An ecosystem asks what combination of actors, institutions, incentives, markets, policies and knowledge is required for the problem to be addressed continuously. That is a more demanding question.

It means recognising that no organisation can build an African childcare system by itself. Government has a role in policy, regulation, financing and public infrastructure. Providers deliver services and understand the realities of families. Caregivers bring professional expertise and lived experience. Researchers generate evidence. Communities bring local knowledge. Businesses can create employment and develop products and services.

Financial institutions can help unlock capital. Civil society can contribute advocacy, accountability and technical expertise. The challenge is not to make these actors identical. It is to make them connected enough to function as an ecosystem. This is central to Uthabiti Africa's approach. The organisation's work is not based on the premise that there is one Kenyan model waiting to be exported across the continent.

Rather, it is about creating platforms, relationships, evidence and practical approaches through which different actors can develop solutions appropriate to their own contexts while learning from one another. That is the logic behind Collaborative Action for Childcare and the wider convening work around childcare. The objective is to make it easier for people working on different parts of the problem to find one another, develop shared priorities, exchange knowledge and build pathways towards scale.

The ambition is therefore not to build one childcare organisation for Africa. It is to help build an African childcare ecosystem capable of continuously building itself. From importing solutions to building African capability There is a deeper issue here than programme design. It is about confidence in African institutions and African knowledge. For too long, development has sometimes treated Africa primarily as a place where solutions are implemented rather than a place where solutions are developed.

Expertise flows into the continent, while knowledge generated within African systems does not always travel with the same authority. Childcare offers an opportunity to change that dynamic. African countries are already experimenting with new ways of approaching workforce development, provider systems, public policy, financing and family support. Practitioners are developing knowledge every day.

Caregivers understand realities that rarely appear in formal research. Governments are testing new policy approaches. Entrepreneurs are responding to emerging demand. The challenge is to connect, document, evaluate and share this knowledge so that it becomes an asset for the wider continent. This does not require turning away from international expertise. It requires a more equal exchange.

Africa should be able to borrow ideas from elsewhere, adapt them where appropriate, reject them where they do not fit and develop entirely new approaches when existing models are inadequate. That is what genuine systems-building looks like. What would a genuinely African childcare future look like? It would not look the same everywhere. There would be different models of provision, different financing arrangements, different workforce pathways and different roles for government and private actors.

But there would be some common characteristics. Childcare would be recognised as essential social and economic infrastructure. Caregivers would be treated as professionals whose knowledge and skills have value. Families would have greater access to affordable and trustworthy services. Providers would have stronger economic foundations. Governments would have the capacity to lead and regulate.

Entrepreneurs and investors would have clearer opportunities to contribute. Communities would have meaningful influence over how services develop. And, crucially, the system would be capable of learning. It would not depend on one organisation having all the answers. It would have mechanisms through which evidence moves between research and practice, between countries and communities, between government and providers, and between successful experiments and the wider system.

That may ultimately be the most important characteristic of a strong African childcare ecosystem: its ability to adapt. Because the future will not stand still. Africa's cities will continue to grow. Employment patterns will change. Climate pressures will affect infrastructure and family life. Technology will create new possibilities. Women's participation in the economy will evolve. Demographic shifts will create new demands.

A childcare system designed for today's conditions but unable to learn will eventually become another constraint. A system capable of learning can evolve with the societies it serves. The opportunity is to build, not simply to replicate The question facing Africa is therefore not whether it can find the perfect childcare model. There probably isn't one. The opportunity is to build the capability to develop better childcare solutions continuously—to test them, learn from them, adapt them and embed what works into institutions and markets that can sustain them.

That requires us to move beyond the idea that scale means taking one successful model and reproducing it everywhere. Sometimes scale means replication. Sometimes it means adaptation. Sometimes it means changing policy. Sometimes it means strengthening a market. Sometimes it means building a workforce institution that did not previously exist. And sometimes it means creating the relationships that allow many different actors to solve different parts of the problem at the same time.

This is why the future of African childcare cannot be designed from the outside in. It must be built from the realities of African families outward, through institutions, markets, communities and partnerships that can sustain it. The continent does not need to choose between learning from the world and building its own solutions. It can do both. But Africa must increasingly see itself not only as a recipient of childcare knowledge, but as a producer of it.

Not only as a place where models are implemented, but as a place where systems are designed. Not only as a collection of countries facing childcare challenges, but as a continent capable of learning collectively from how those challenges are being addressed. That is the opportunity before us. Not to import an African childcare model, but to build African capacity to create the childcare systems that Africa needs.
And if we can build that capacity, the future of childcare will no longer depend on finding a single solution. It will depend on having an ecosystem capable of continually creating better ones.

title: From Conversation to Collective Action: What the Africa Childcare Forum Enabled
author: Asayya Imaya
excerpt: Following the 2nd Africa Childcare Forum in Mombasa, the question was no longer whether we could bring the childcare ecosystem together. It was what we could accomplish when we did. Blog #8 From Conversation to…
paragraphs: Following the 2nd Africa Childcare Forum in Mombasa, the question was no longer whether we could bring the childcare ecosystem together. It was what we could accomplish when we did. Blog #8 From Conversation to Collective Action: What Did the Africa Childcare Forum Enable? Africa is talking about childcare more than it has in the past. Governments are developing policies and strategies.

Researchers are producing evidence. Organisations are testing new approaches. Advocates are calling for greater investment. Businesses are increasingly recognising the relationship between childcare, women’s economic participation and productivity. Caregivers are seeking greater recognition of their work. Families continue to make difficult choices every day about how to care for young children while earning a living.

There is growing recognition that childcare matters. But recognition is not transformation. Across the continent, the gap between attention to childcare and the systems available to families remains significant. Investment is fragmented, the workforce remains largely informal and undervalued, providers face difficult economics, and promising innovations often struggle to move beyond individual projects.

Most importantly, the many actors working on different parts of the childcare system do not always have the mechanisms to work together around shared priorities. The question is therefore changing. It is no longer simply how do we get childcare onto the agenda? It is how do we turn growing recognition into collective action capable of changing the system? That was the opportunity presented by the Africa Childcare Forum.

From convening to collective action When Uthabiti Africa was established in 2019, childcare was being advanced by a relatively small number of organisations and institutions. We believed that the scale and complexity of the challenge required more actors to participate. From a market-systems perspective, one of the first things we did was convene. And we convened deliberately. In 2022, we brought stakeholders together through the first Policy Conference on ECCED in Kenya.

In 2023, we launched the Women in Childcare Forum. In 2024, we convened the Collaborative Action for Childcare Annual Conference. In 2025, we hosted the first Africa Childcare Forum, followed by the second Women in Childcare Forum. In 2026, we convened the 2nd Africa Childcare Forum in Mombasa. The significance of this journey is not simply the number of events held. It is what has happened around them: more actors entering the conversation, stronger relationships being formed, new areas of collaboration emerging, and a growing recognition that childcare cannot be advanced through isolated interventions.

Convening was the starting point. The next challenge is to make that growing ecosystem more capable of acting together. The childcare challenge requires different actors to see the same system Childcare is shaped by decisions made in many different places. A policymaker thinks about regulation, public services and national priorities. A caregiver experiences the realities of the workforce.

A provider thinks about costs, demand and the viability of the service. A parent thinks about affordability, trust, safety and quality. A researcher brings evidence. An entrepreneur sees unmet demand and opportunities for innovation. An investor considers risk and potential returns. All of these perspectives matter. None is sufficient on its own. This is why childcare cannot be solved through a series of disconnected programmes.

A country can train more caregivers without creating a viable workforce system. It can establish childcare centres without addressing provider economics. It can develop strong policies without the financing and institutional capacity required for implementation. It can support promising innovations without creating pathways for those innovations to reach more families. The challenge is not simply to find interventions that work.

It is to understand what needs to change around those interventions so that they can become sustainable, accessible and capable of reaching scale. That requires people who normally work in different spaces to see the system together. The Forum created that opportunity. What happens after the Forum matters most Conferences often produce strong conversations and broad agreement. Everyone agrees that childcare matters.

Everyone agrees that investment should increase. Everyone agrees that caregivers deserve better conditions. Everyone agrees that governments have a critical role. The harder questions come afterwards. Who will do what? What resources will be committed? Which institutions will take responsibility? What policy needs to change? What capability needs to be built? Which partnerships need to be formed?

What should be different twelve months from now? These questions sat at the centre of ACF Mombasa 2026. Collective action does not mean that every organisation does the same thing. It means that different actors understand their contribution and how it connects to the contributions of others. A government may strengthen policy implementation. A training institution may develop recognised workforce pathways.

Providers may work together to improve quality and professional standards. Businesses may explore childcare solutions for their employees. Financial institutions may develop appropriate products for providers. Researchers may address critical evidence gaps. Development partners may align resources behind nationally owned priorities. The important thing is that these contributions connect.

A collection of commitments is not collective action. Collective action happens when different contributions reinforce a shared objective. Building the infrastructure for collaboration One of the lessons from Uthabiti's work is that collaboration does not happen simply because people have good intentions. It needs infrastructure. Networks, technical working groups, policy dialogues, professional associations, learning platforms and collaborative initiatives create the relationships and mechanisms through which people can continue working together after a meeting ends.

This is an important role for the Collaborative Action for Childcare (CAC). The purpose of CAC is not simply to convene organisations around childcare. It is to provide a platform through which actors can identify shared priorities, exchange evidence, develop solutions, learn from implementation and work towards scale. The Africa Childcare Forum created energy and alignment. Platforms such as CAC continued to provide a way to sustain that energy.

This distinction matters because systems do not change through events alone. They change when relationships, institutions, policies, markets, capabilities and incentives begin to work differently over time. The Forum was therefore understood as part of a longer process—not as an endpoint. Who gets to shape the future? Collective action also requires us to ask who is included. Caregivers cannot be treated simply as recipients of conference reports and training when they are the people delivering care every day, those who know what works in practice.

Parents cannot be viewed only as beneficiaries when they understand the realities of affordability, trust and access. Fathers should not be looked at as secondary caregivers when evidence shows they are increasingly engaged in childcare. Providers cannot be treated merely as service delivery channels when they understand the economics of childcare. Communities possess knowledge about what works in their own contexts.

Their participation must be meaningful. That is why for Uthabiti, our ecosystem building work intentionally ensures childcare workers are in the room whether it is during the ACF or the childcare worker training curriculum. A stronger childcare ecosystem is therefore not simply one with more organisations around the table. It is one in which more actors have the capability and agency to shape what happens next.

From Africa learning from others to Africa learning from itself The Forum also provided an opportunity to strengthen how Africa contributed to the global childcare conversation. International evidence and experience are valuable. But African countries should not be positioned primarily as consumers of models developed elsewhere. There is significant knowledge being generated here. Governments are developing new policy approaches.

Organisations are testing workforce and market models. Providers are adapting to challenging economic environments. Researchers are documenting emerging evidence. Communities are developing locally relevant responses. The opportunity is to connect that knowledge across countries and make it more visible. The question should not only be, “What can Africa learn from the world?” It should also be, “What can Africa learn from itself?” That requires sharing both success and failure.

It requires countries to learn from one another without assuming that one model can simply be copied elsewhere. The ambition should be to build African capacity to develop childcare systems suited to African realities, while contributing African experience and evidence to the wider global conversation. From conversation to action The measure of ACF Mombasa 2026 ultimately lay in what happened after the Forum.

We should leave with clearer priorities about the structural barriers that matter most. We should leave with stronger relationships between actors who need to work together. We should leave with practical commitments and partnerships capable of carrying those commitments forward. We should see clearer pathways for action around workforce development, policy, financing, markets, investment and scale.

And we should have stronger mechanisms through which progress can continue to be discussed, measured and adapted. That is what moving from conversation to collective action means. It does not mean that a single forum will solve Africa's childcare challenge. It will not. But it can help create the conditions for a stronger ecosystem—one in which more actors are capable of contributing, learning, investing, innovating and leading.

That is the direction in which Uthabiti's journey has been moving since 2019. The objective has never been to build an organisation that owns the childcare agenda. It has been to help build an ecosystem capable of carrying that agenda forward. The next chapter has to be collective Africa's childcare challenge is too large for business as usual. It is too large for isolated projects, and certainly too large for one organisation.

The past several years have been about bringing more actors into the ecosystem. The next chapter is about what that ecosystem can do together. Following the 2nd Africa Childcare Forum in Mombasa in 2026, the question was no longer simply whether we could bring the sector together. The Forum demonstrated that we could. The question is: What will we do with the collective strength we are building?

The 2nd Africa Childcare Forum helped move the conversation from recognition towards action, from individual initiatives towards shared priorities, and towards the partnerships, commitments and systems needed to take childcare to scale. The next chapter of Africa's childcare story cannot be written by a few. It has to be built by many—and built together.
